transcript.text: I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

That's a clear brief, and there's a lot you can do with it. One honest caveat before anything: the value list is only as good as the list behind it — with hand-typed names, branch-by-branch accounts and the same firms in both systems, the same contractor could appear 5–10 times and be spread across the top-150 cut. So the first real piece of work is merging accounts into one record per firm; everything else sits on top of that. I've set up the options accordingly.

The natural order is the merged list first, the LTV ranking second, and the forecast as a follow-up once you've seen the ranking — but you're free to pick whichever gets you to the decision fastest.

One question that decides how the merge is done: besides the account number and the hand-typed name, does either account master hold an address, a VAT or tax number, or a phone number for the firms?

choices.title: One clean firm-level customer list
choices.what: Merge the two account lists into one record per firm: match hand-typed names and the same firm buying from both companies, roll site/branch accounts up to the firm level, and combine the three years of invoices per firm. You get: A single de-duplicated customer master (~how many firms you really have) with each firm's full invoice history under one number — the foundation the rest needs. Trade-off: Produces no ranking yet, and matching quality depends on what identifying fields the systems hold beyond names. Effort: A few days of data work, mostly matching rules and a review list of uncertain pairs for your team to sign off.

choices.title: LTV score and ranked top-150 list
choices.what: From the merged list, score every firm's lifetime value from three years of invoices — total spend, recency, trend (growing or shrinking), and breadth across branches — then rank all firms and mark the top ~150 plus the borderline band your reps will want to argue about. You get: A decision-ready list: who gets a key-account manager, who sits just below the line, and which promising small-account firms the reps would have missed. Trade-off: Scores are based on the last three years; it rewards proven spend rather than predicted future growth. Effort: Starts from the merged list; the ranking itself is quick once the merge exists.

choices.title: Forecast next year's value per firm
choices.what: You get: A forward-looking score that complements the historical LTV ranking and answers the 'ones they miss' part of your goal more directly. Trade-off: More to build and to trust; the prediction is only as good as the merged data underneath, and it adds a model your team must learn to read. Effort: Larger project, in one phase, on top of the merged list.

Cancellations cost us a lot, so I plan to ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled and keep the normal terms for everyone else. Please build the model that decides who must pay the deposit. The table I shared has one row per booking: booking date, travel date, destination, the customer's nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether free cancellation was offered, and whether the booking was cancelled. From what I have seen in our reports, nationality tells the most about who cancels, so I expect it to be the main input. The website would apply the rule automatically at checkout. [shares bookings.csv]

You ordered the build, so it's started: a model on your 1,500 bookings that scores each new booking's chance of being cancelled, so your website can ask the deposit from the ones that score high. Here's what I understood and what happens next. What the problem really is: this is a policy decision wearing a prediction costume. You're not only asking which bookings cancel — you're asking which ones get moved to non-refundable terms: how many you flag, on which signals, and whether the rule holds up when a European customer looks at it. The approach: your instinct that nationality is the main input is one we'll test, not assume. Two things I saw in your table: (1) you have customer_id, so we can build each customer's own cancellation history — that is usually a stronger and fairer signal than nationality; (2) because you sell into the EU, a rule that visibly sorts people by nationality invites non-discrimination challenges, and your nationality differences are likely just the mix of channel, lead time, price and free-cancellation that each group happens to book with. Train with a holdout: fit on older bookings, test on the newest, and check the model genuinely separates cancellations — and be honest about how far 1,500 rows carries the threshold. 3. Calibration: the cancellation rate in each probability band, so we pick the deposit cutoff together. 4. Fairness check: the rule with and without nationality; your call on what ships. 5. Handoff: a scoring rule your checkout can call, plus a short report on who gets flagged and why. Next: DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now, and you'll get the holdout result, the probability-band chart and the fairness comparison in this chat once it has run.

decision.value: Which bookings at checkout must pay a non-refundable deposit vs. which keep normal terms, applied automatically by the website
decision.quote: ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled

constraints.quote: nationality tells the most about who cancels

findings.text: Applying a non-refundable deposit triggered by nationality to EU consumers is exposed to EU non-discrimination law (Art. 18 TFEU, Unfair Contract Terms Directive 93/13/EEC) and to GDPR Article 22, which bars solely automated decisions with a significant financial effect without a human-in-the-loop. transcript.text: I am the business intelligence analyst at a retailer that sells in its own shops and online across the UAE. The chief executive wants one weekly revenue dashboard, by region, channel and product category, that everyone trusts. Last month the sales director reported revenue about nine percent higher than finance did for the same weeks, and each says the other is wrong. Both teams start from the export I shared: one row per order with an order id, the order date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer id. The status column shows how each order ended. I would like the dashboard built from this table so I can present it at Monday's management meeting. The chief executive will use it to judge the regional managers. [shares sales.csv]

## What the problem actually is

The decision the CEO faces on Monday is: *which regional managers are performing well or poorly, and is the gap between regions real or an artefact of how the number was built?* The unit of analysis is one order (your 2,020 rows), the moment is a rolling or calendar week anchored on **order_date**, and the output is a single weekly revenue figure broken down by region, channel, and product category.

What is **known**: the export you shared, its eight columns, the fact that both the sales director and finance start from *this same file*, and the size of their disagreement (about nine percent on the same weeks).

What is **not known** (and is almost certainly the whole problem): what values sit in **status** and which of them each team counts as "revenue." Sales may total every row regardless of whether the order was later cancelled, returned, or is still pending; finance may only total confirmed-and-settled orders. Neither team is "wrong" — they are applying a different cut to the same column. A secondary unknown is whether **amount** is gross, net of VAT, net of discounts, or net of refunds; if the two teams disagree on that too, the gap could be tax-related rather than status-related. I do not know the date span those 2,020 rows cover, how many regions or channels exist, or whether the retailer works on calendar weeks or a fiscal week.

No predictive model is needed. This is a **definition and reconciliation** problem, not a forecasting or classification problem.

## Approaches on the table

| Approach | What it gives | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Explicit rule + dashboard (no model).** Sit down with sales and finance, list every status value, agree which constitute "recognised revenue," hard-code that rule into a computed column, build the dashboard on it. | One number both teams can defend. Transparent to the CEO. Reconcilable to the ledger. | A few hours of discussion plus a single aggregation query. No infrastructure beyond what you already use to read the CSV. |
| **B. Statistical anomaly flag.** Let the dashboard show every order and highlight the ones that drive the gap between the two teams' totals. | Diagnostic visibility. | Still requires you to know *which* rule each team used first, so it does not remove the definitional disagreement. More UI complexity for the CEO, who wants one number, not a forensic view. |
| **C. Predictive / ML model** (e.g., predict "will this order become recognised revenue?"). | A probabilistic per-order flag. | Overkill: the status column already tells you the outcome. You would be modelling a known categorical label. Adds a black-box layer the CEO cannot interrogate at Monday's meeting. |

## Chosen approach and plan

I choose **A**, reinforced by a short diagnostic step (a lightweight version of B used only for *you*, not for the CEO). The steps, in order:

**Step 1 – Profile the file (you, ~1–2 h).**
Read the 2,020 rows. List every distinct value in *status* and its row count. Check the min/max of *order_date* to know how many weeks the file spans. Check for nulls, duplicate *order_id*s, negative *amount* values (returns?), and whether *amount* looks like a pre- or post-VAT figure (e.g., multiples of 1.05). You need no external data; this is the table you already have.

**Step 2 – Reconstruct both teams' numbers (you, ~1 h).**
Using the status distribution from Step 1, try every plausible subset: sum *amount* where status is in {confirmed, completed}; where it is not in {cancelled, returned}; where it is "all rows"; where it excludes *pending*. Whichever subset reproduces the sales director's figure and whichever reproduces finance's figure pinpoints the exact disagreement. You now know, concretely, what the nine percent is made of.

**Step 3 – Agree the revenue rule (you + sales director + finance lead, 30-min call or email thread).**
Present the Step 2 finding: "Your number includes pending orders; mine does not." Propose the rule that matches the finance ledger (that is the number the CEO can be held to). Get the rule in one sentence, in writing, e.g. *"Weekly revenue = sum of amount where status is in {confirmed, completed} and order_date falls in the reporting week."* If the CEO wants pending orders visible, they appear in a secondary panel, not in the headline number.

**Step 4 – Build the weekly aggregate (you, ~1–2 h).**
One query / script: filter to the agreed status set, group by ISO week (or the retailer's fiscal week — confirm with finance), *region*, *channel*, *product_category*, sum *amount*. Output is a small table: week × region × channel × category → revenue. Attach the same file every Monday; the dashboard refreshes.

**Step 5 – Build the dashboard (you, ~half a day depending on your tool).**
One page, top-to-bottom:
- **Headline KPI:** total revenue for the selected week.
- **Slicers / filters:** region, channel, product category.
- **Main table or treemap:** revenue by the three dimensions.
- **Small "transparency" panel (this is what makes it trusted):** a stacked bar or mini-table showing, for the selected week, how many orders and how much *amount* fall into each status *excluded* from the headline. The CEO sees that returns and cancellations exist but are ring-fenced.
- **Week-over-week delta** on the headline so the CEO sees movement, not just a static number.

**Step 6 – Validate before Monday (you, ~1 h).**
Pick one week from last month. Run your aggregate. Hand the number to the finance lead and ask, "Does this match your ledger for that week?" If yes, the rule is correct. If not, you have a residual discrepancy (tax treatment, a late-dated order, a refund posted to a different week) and you fix the rule before the meeting. Do not present until it matches.

**Step 7 – Present and hand off (Monday).**
Show the dashboard, state the revenue rule in one line on the slide, and note that the transparency panel is there if anyone wants to see what is *not* in the headline. Distribute the underlying aggregated CSV so regional managers can check their own row without re-running the query.

## When to stop

You stop when three things are true:
1. The headline number for a test week matches finance's ledger exactly.
2. The CEO (or their delegate) has read the one-sentence revenue rule and said "that is what I want."
3. The dashboard renders correctly with the 2,020-row file (or its weekly refresh) without manual edits.

If any of those fails, you are not done; go back to the step that failed.

## What I am assuming (not told to me)

- The nine percent gap is driven by the **status** column, not by a different date field, a different *amount* definition, or missing rows in one team's extract. Step 2 confirms or refutes this.
- The 2,020 rows are the complete population for the period in question (no separate "returns table" or "adjustments table" that finance pulls in). If such a table exists, the rule in Step 3 must reference it.
- "Region" in the file maps one-to-one to the regional managers the CEO will judge. If one region is split between two managers, the dashboard needs a second mapping layer.
- The retailer uses a standard ISO or calendar week; if there is a bespoke fiscal calendar, Step 4 uses that instead.

Nothing here requires a model. It requires one conversation, one rule, one query, and one honest panel that shows what is left out. That is what makes the number one the CEO can use to judge people without being accused of cherry-picking.

I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

## What the problem actually is

**The decision.** You need to pick roughly 150 names from a combined pool of about 6,500 raw accounts (your ~4,000 plus the acquired firm's ~2,500) and say: "these get a dedicated key-account manager." That is a ranking-and-cutoff decision, not a prediction in the abstract.

**Who will use the result.** You, your sales-management layer, and the KAMs themselves. The list drives headcount deployment and visit frequency, so it has to be defensible to the people on the ground, not just statistically tidy.

**The unit of analysis.** A *consolidated trading entity*—one contractor, one firm—regardless of how many site-level or branch-level accounts it currently holds across the two systems. Right now you do not have that unit. You have 6,500 rows that overlap, split, and mis-name the same firms.

**The moment it concerns.** The next KAM allocation cycle (I assume quarterly or annual, but you haven't told me). The model looks backward over the three years of invoices you have and projects a short forward window (I assume 12 months, since that is what a KAM's year of coverage looks like).

**What you know.** For each of the two systems: three years of invoices carrying an account number, a date, and an amount. Hand-typed company names. No shared key between the two systems.

**What you do not know (and I am flagging, not assuming away):**
- Whether "amount" is net of tax, before or after discounts, and whether product-line or margin data exists anywhere in the system.
- Which accounts are still active, which went dormant, and which were closed at acquisition.
- Any cost-to-serve information (credit terms, delivery frequency, returns, disputes).
- Current KAM assignments, if any, at either company.
- A forecast horizon beyond "the next period."
- Whether the 2,500 accounts from the competitor include any that were already your customers before the acquisition (you say many firms bought from both, which I read as overlap, but I don't know the overlap rate).

All of these gaps matter for the model's accuracy, but none of them stop you from building a useful first pass. I will say where each gap would change the answer.

---

## Approaches on the table

### 1. No model at all – a weighted historical-spend list
Consolidate the accounts (see Phase 1 below), sum each entity's 36-month spend, weight the most recent 12 months more heavily (say, 60/40 or 70/30), rank, take the top 150.

- **Cost.** A few days of data wrangling in a spreadsheet or a light database script. No modelling skill needed.
- **What it gives.** A defensible "who has given us the most money recently" list.
- **What it misses.** An account that is small today but has been growing 40 % a quarter. A contractor whose three site-accounts each look mid-tier but together are a top-30 entity. A firm that went quiet after a project finished but is likely to re-tender. In short, it will largely reproduce what your reps already see as "the big ones." You told me the model's job is to find what they *miss*; this approach will not do that.

### 2. A probabilistic CLV model (BG/NBD + Gamma-Gamma, or a close variant)
Treat each consolidated account as a customer with a purchase process. BG/NBD estimates the probability the account will still be transacting in the next period; Gamma-Gamma estimates how much it will spend conditional on staying. Multiply them for an expected 12-month value.

- **Cost.** A few weeks. The heavy part is not the model (it is two small, well-known formulas) but the data preparation: clean invoices, handle the entity-resolution step, decide how to treat the overlap accounts, and agree on what "amount" means. You will need someone comfortable in Python or R. No rare data needed—your three years of date-and-amount rows are exactly what these models want.
- **What it gives.** A forward-looking score that rewards accounts with a strong *and recent* purchase cadence, and penalises ones that have gone quiet. It naturally surfaces the "sleeping giant" accounts your reps overlook because the last invoice was six months ago on a big project.
- **Limit.** It assumes the purchase process is roughly Poisson/lognormal, which is a decent first approximation for construction-materials buying but will under-represent very lumpy, project-based spend. It also cannot see into the future; it extrapolates the recent past.

### 3. A supervised / gradient-boosting CLV model
Build features (recency, frequency, monetary, trend slope, number of distinct sites, share of wallet between the two legacy systems, etc.), label the last 3–6 months as the "target" value, train a gradient-boosted tree or a survival model, and score the remaining accounts.

- **Cost.** More weeks, a data-scientist or analyst, more feature-engineering judgment. You will spend time arguing with yourself about leakage (using the future as a label and then "predicting" it).
- **What it gives.** Can capture interactions (e.g., "a firm that was small on your list but large on the competitor's list and has been buying from both in the last six months is consolidating spend"). Potentially the most accurate.
- **Limit.** Harder to explain to a KAM who asks "why is this account on the list?" Three years of data with roughly 6,500 entities is a thin dataset for a tree ensemble; you risk overfitting. You need margin or cost data to make it truly decision-useful, and you have not told me you have it.

### 4. A hybrid score (my recommendation, detailed below)
Entity resolution first, then a transparent weighted score that blends a historical-value component, a recency/growth component, and a consolidation signal. No black box. A single page of arithmetic per account.

- **Cost.** Comparable to option 2 in data work, less in modelling time. One or two analysts, a few weeks including the messy de-duplication.
- **What it gives.** You get most of the "find the sleeping giants" benefit of option 2 with the explainability of option 1, plus an explicit flag for accounts that were split across the two systems (which is a commercial opportunity in itself, not just a data artefact).

---

## The plan I would run

### Phase 1 – Consolidate the accounts (the hard, unglamorous 60 %)

This is where most of the project risk lives, and it is not a modelling problem.

1. **Export the raw files.** You said nothing is exported yet. Get, for each system, the full three-year invoice table (account number, date, amount) and the account master (account number, hand-typed name, any address or site field you have). Agree on a common date format and currency before anything else.
2. **De-duplicate within each system.** A contractor with five site-accounts in your system is one entity. Use the hand-typed names plus, if you have them, addresses, VAT/tax IDs, or registration numbers. Because names are typed by hand, you will need fuzzy string matching (edit distance, token overlap) combined with a rule: if two accounts share an address or a tax ID, they are the same entity. Build a mapping table: *entity ID → list of legacy account numbers, system of origin.*
3. **Merge across the two systems.** Apply the same fuzzy-match logic between your 4,000 and their 2,500. Flag accounts that appear in both. You said many firms bought from both; expect a meaningful overlap. For each match, keep both invoice streams but assign a single entity ID.
4. **Resolve the messy ones manually.** The automated pass will get most of it. The ambiguous cases (similar names, no shared address, only one invoice in common) need a person. Budget a few days of your credit or customer-service team reviewing the unmatched and the uncertain. You do not need 100 % purity; you need the top-200 entities to be right, because those are the ones in play for a KAM.
5. **Produce the consolidated transaction file.** One row per invoice: *entity ID, date, amount, source system.* You now have roughly 4,000–5,000 distinct entities (the exact number depends on how many of the 6,500 collapse), each with a three-year purchase history.

*What you need:* two data extractors or IT support to export, one analyst comfortable with string-matching in SQL or Python, and a business person to adjudicate the ambiguous pairs. *How you check it:* spot-check 30 random consolidated entities against your own knowledge of the customer base; count how many should have been one entity or two. Aim for fewer than 3–4 mistakes in 30. Re-run if worse.

### Phase 2 – Build the score

For each consolidated entity, compute from the three-year invoice stream:

- **H (historical value):** total amount over the full 36 months, and total over the last 12 months.
- **R (recency):** months since the last invoice.
- **G (growth / trend):** compare the last-12-month total to the prior-12-month total. A ratio or a simple slope.
- **C (consolidation signal):** a binary or small flag—did this entity appear in both legacy systems in the last 12 months? If so, it is actively buying from you *and* from what is now also you, which is both a risk (they may be consolidating with a third party) and an opportunity (a KAM can lock the relationship).
- **N (breadth):** number of distinct site-accounts feeding this entity. More sites often means a larger firm and more future tender surface.

Then combine them into a single score. The simplest workable formula is a weighted z-score or percentile blend, for example: 40 % last-12-month value, 20 % 36-month value, 15 % recency (inverse), 15 % growth, 10 % breadth/consolidation. The exact weights are a business judgment—sit with your sales-management team and ask them to argue the weights. Do not let the numbers pick them for you.

If you have the appetite and the data, overlay the BG/NBD survival probability as an additional multiplier: an account that has had no invoice in 14 months gets its score damped by the estimated probability it will transact again in the next 12. This is the single biggest improvement over a pure spend ranking, because it is what catches the "they went quiet after their last project" accounts your reps are not watching.

*What you need:* the consolidated transaction file from Phase 1; an analyst who can write the scoring in a script (not a black-box model, a formula you can print on a page); one session with sales-management to set and sanity-check the weights. *How you check it:* the score should be monotonically reasonable—if I look at the top 5 and the bottom 5, I should not be surprised. The top 5 should include at least one account your reps did *not* name when you asked them "who are your top 20?" (that is the whole point).

### Phase 3 – Validate against the reps and against the overlap

1. **Blind-spot test.** Ask each sales rep (or the sales-management layer) to list, independently of the model, the 20 accounts they believe deserve a KAM. Overlay their names on the model's top 150. Count:
   - How many of the model's top 150 are *not* on any rep's list. These are the "ones they miss" you asked the model to find. If the number is zero or one, the model is just re-stating what the reps already see and is not earning its keep.
   - How many of the reps' named accounts are *outside* the top 150. Review each one manually; if it is genuinely high-value and the score missed it, find out why (wrong weight? a data gap in Phase 1?) and adjust.
2. **Overlap check.** For the entities that existed in both systems, confirm the merged invoice history looks right (no double-counting, no missing months around the acquisition date). If the acquisition was mid-year, you may have a step-change in spend for those entities that will distort the 36-month total; you may want to weight the post-acquisition period separately.
3. **Sensitivity check.** Nudge each weight by ±5 percentage points and see how much the top-150 membership changes. If a small weight change swaps 40 accounts in and out, the list is fragile and the weights are not well-grounded. Iterate with the team until the list is stable.

### Phase 4 – Decide and lock the 150

- Cut the ranked list at 150.
- Review the 151st-to-180th band as a "next-year pipeline" so you are not surprised when an account tips over.
- Flag the consolidation-signal accounts explicitly: these need a KAM not because they are the biggest today, but because the relationship is in flux post-acquisition and a single owner prevents the customer from splitting orders between two sales teams that don't talk to each other.
- Document, for each account on the list, *why* it is there (one line: "top-decile 12-month spend," or "small but +60 % growth and present in both legacy systems"). A KAM will accept a list with a reason; they will not accept a list with a z-score.

*When to stop.* You stop when:
- The blind-spot test shows the model is adding genuine names the reps missed (you told me that is the point),
- The top-150 membership is stable under small weight changes,
- Your sales-management team can look at the top 50 and say "yes, that's who we want a KAM on" without the model having to justify itself with jargon,
- You have a named owner for the Phase 1 de-duplication file so it can be re-run when the next competitor is acquired or when the data is refreshed annually.

You do not need to keep tuning. You need a process that runs once a year (or once a quarter if your cycle is quarterly), takes about two to three weeks end-to-end, and produces a defensible 150-name list with a one-line reason per name.

- I have assumed the three-year window at both companies starts at the same calendar date. If the competitor's data goes back further or less, the 36-month comparison is not like-for-like and I would restrict both to the common window.
- I have assumed you do not have margin, cost-to-serve, or return-rate data available. If you do, the score improves materially (an account that spends a lot but returns 15 % and gets 60-day credit is not worth a KAM the way a 40 %-margin, 30-day account is). Tell me if you can pull that and I would add it as a sixth factor.
- I have assumed the 150-KAM figure is fixed for this cycle. If it is a budget that flexes ±20 %, the cutoff logic changes slightly (you can use a threshold on the score rather than a hard rank).

Hand-typed names, multi-site accounts, and two different numbering schemes mean the consolidation step will be 60–70 % of the calendar time and most of the political friction (two sales teams both wanting their "big accounts" to show up). Cancellations cost us a lot, so I plan to ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled and keep the normal terms for everyone else. Please build the model that decides who must pay the deposit. The table I shared has one row per booking: booking date, travel date, destination, the customer's nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether free cancellation was offered, and whether the booking was cancelled. # The problem in plain terms

**The decision.** At the moment a customer reaches the checkout page, the system must pick one of two terms: "pay a non-refundable deposit now" or "standard refundable terms." The choice is made per booking, not per customer, and it is irreversible once the booking is confirmed.

**Who acts on it.** The website executes the rule automatically. You (revenue manager) set the policy and the threshold; no human looks at the score in the moment.

**The unit and the moment.** One row in `bookings.csv` is one booking. The prediction must be made *at checkout*, using only fields that exist before the booking is sealed: booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead-time-in-days, price, and whether free cancellation was offered. You do **not** know the customer's mood, their creditworthiness, or whether they will change plans. The 1,500 rows in the file are past bookings whose outcome (cancelled = 1/0) is already known; that is your training material.

**What you know.** The full history of 1,500 bookings with the columns listed. You also have domain reports suggesting nationality is a strong predictor of cancellation.

**What is not known (and is the whole point).** Whether a *new* booking will end up cancelled. That is the binary label the model must estimate.

**A flag I have to raise before anything else.** You told me nationality "tells the most about who cancels" and that you expect it to be "the main input." I take that as your observation of the data. What I must separate is the *legal and reputational* consequence of encoding nationality into a pricing term. For your European customers, EU consumer-protection and anti-discrimination rules (and the national laws of 27 member states) can make it illegal to attach a less favourable financial condition on the basis of a customer's nationality. In the UAE the framework is different, but your website serves both markets and any single rule must satisfy the stricter regime. Applying a deposit because a customer is, say, British while a customer of another nationality gets normal terms for the same product is the kind of treatment that has triggered fines and class actions in EU e-commerce. I will come back to this in the plan.

---

# Approaches on the table

| # | Approach | What it gives you | What it costs |
|---|----------|-------------------|--------------|
| 1 | **No model – a fixed rule you set by hand** (e.g., "if lead-time < 14 days AND free cancellation offered, require deposit"). | You can ship it this week. Zero ML infrastructure. Fully auditable in a court or a regulator. | You will miss patterns that involve interactions among three or more variables; you will over- or under-deposit on many bookings. |
| 2 | **Logistic regression** on the 8 features (minus or plus nationality – see flag). | Probabilistic score 0-1 you can threshold. Coefficients tell you *why* a booking is flagged. Runs in milliseconds on any server. With 1,500 rows and 8 predictors it is well within the data's capacity. | Linear-only: it cannot capture "short lead-time *and* European destination *and* no free cancellation is especially bad" unless you add interaction terms by hand. |
| 3 | **Single shallow decision tree** (depth 2-3). | Same probability output, but automatically finds the interaction you would have to add by hand. The resulting "if lead-time < 20 → if destination = beach → flag" is trivially explained to a customer-service agent. | With 1,500 rows, a tree deeper than 3 over-fits; you must cap depth and prune. Slightly less stable than regression across resamples. |
| 4 | **Ensemble (gradient-boosted trees, random forest).** | Marginally better AUC (typically +1-3 points on a dataset this size). | Over-kill for 1,500 rows; the gain is within the noise of a single 80/20 split. Harder to explain to a regulator or a customer. Adds a dependency and tuning time you do not need. |

Given that the website applies the rule *automatically at checkout* (so speed and a hard-coded threshold matter), that the dataset is 1,500 rows (so complexity buys you almost nothing), and that a regulator or a customer's lawyer may need to read the logic, I would not go past option 3.

---

# What I would choose and the plan, step by step

**Chosen approach:** a **logistic regression** (option 2) as the workhorse, cross-checked against a **depth-2 decision tree** (option 3) as a sanity check and as the "plain-language" version you can show in a FAQ. Both are small, fast, and explainable. I would **not** include nationality as a direct feature (see the flag above). If you insist on using it, the minimum is to encode it only as "market = UAE-resident vs. EU-resident" (a two-level variable tied to the *sales channel / website locale*, not to a passport field), and to get legal sign-off before go-live. I assume you have a legal team you can consult; if not, treat that as a blocking step.

### Step 0 – Data hygiene (half a day)
- Confirm `cancelled` is truly 0/1 (the schema labels it "numeric, small code or flag").
- `price` is typed *categorical* in the schema you shared. If it is actually a continuous amount, re-type it as numeric; if it is a price tier (e.g., "economy / business / suite"), keep it categorical but confirm the levels.
- Drop `booking_id` and `customer_id` from the feature set (they are identifiers, not predictors). If `customer_id` lets you count "this customer has booked with us before," derive a binary `repeat_customer` flag and use *that*; do not feed raw IDs to the model.
- Decide the training window: you said "since last year" for Europe, so the 1,500 rows span roughly a year. If there is a seasonality spike (Ramadan, summer), note it; you may want to stratify by season in the split.

### Step 1 – EDA to confirm or challenge your nationality hypothesis (a day)
- Compute the cancellation rate by each feature (destination, channel, lead-time bucket, free-cancellation flag, nationality, price tier).
- You told me nationality is the strongest single predictor. I expect you to see that, but you will probably also see that **lead_time_days** and **free_cancellation** are very strong and, crucially, *actionable and legally clean*. The question is not "which feature has the highest univariate rate" but "which combination, *excluding nationality*, gets me close enough to the optimum."
- Check the class balance: if, say, 8 % of 1,500 bookings were cancelled (≈ 120 rows), that is workable for logistic regression but you will want to report precision and recall at your chosen threshold, not just accuracy.

### Step 2 – Feature design (half a day)
- Keep: `lead_time_days` (numeric), `destination` (categorical, one-hot or target-encoded given 1,500 rows), `channel`, `free_cancellation`, `price` (re-typed per Step 0), `repeat_customer` (if derivable), and **`market`** (UAE vs. EU, derived from channel or site locale – *not* from passport).
- Drop: `nationality` (legal risk), `booking_date` and `travel_date` as raw timestamps (use `lead_time_days` and a `season` flag instead), `customer_id`, `booking_id`.
- You do **not** need many rows to justify this: 1,500 is enough for ≤ 8-10 features in a logistic model.

### Step 3 – Model fit and validation (a day)
- 70/30 (or 80/20) train/test split, stratified by `cancelled`.
- Fit logistic regression with L1 (Lasso) regularisation so it automatically drops weak features and gives you a sparse, explainable coefficient table.
- Fit a depth-2 decision tree on the same split as a cross-check.
- Report on the **test** set only: AUC, and at the specific threshold you will use in production, precision (of the flagged group, how many truly cancelled) and recall (of all cancellations, how many you caught). Also report the false-positive rate: the share of *non-cancelling* customers who get the deposit, because that is the goodwill cost.
- **Honesty check:** with 1,500 rows and a base rate around 8-12 %, the confidence interval on AUC will be roughly ±0.04-0.06. Do not compare models to four decimal places.

### Step 4 – Choose the operating threshold (with you, not the model)
- The model gives a probability. You choose the cut-off. The business question is: "At what cancellation-probability does the expected deposit revenue exceed the expected loss in customer goodwill / lost future bookings?" That is your number to pick; the model only tells you how many bookings fall above each candidate threshold.
- Agree with the customer-service team what the explanation script will be ("We ask for a deposit on last-minute bookings to X" rather than "Our algorithm flagged you").

### Step 5 – Implement at checkout (engineering, a few days)
- Serialise the logistic-regression weights (a handful of coefficients) into the checkout microservice. No GPU, no big inference stack. A 10-feature dot product plus a sigmoid runs in microseconds.
- The depth-2 tree can be hard-coded as nested if/else as a fallback or for the "why" shown to the customer.
- Log every decision (booking_id, feature values, probability, which side of the threshold) for your own monitoring and for any future regulatory inquiry.

### Step 6 – Go live and monitor (ongoing)
- Week 1: run in "shadow mode" – the model *scores* every checkout but does not actually charge the deposit. Compare its flags against what a human manager would have decided.
- After sign-off: switch on. Track weekly: (a) cancellation rate among deposited vs. non-deposited bookings, (b) deposit-recovery rate, (c) customer-complaint rate and repeat-booking rate among those who were asked for a deposit.
- **Stop / retrain trigger:** if the false-positive rate (non-cancelling customers hit with a deposit) exceeds the level you agreed in Step 4, or if the overall cancellation rate shifts by more than a few points (new destination launched, post-pandemic behaviour change), retrain on the accumulated data. With 1,500 historical rows you are thin; after 3-6 months of live logging you will have more, and the model will tighten.

### When to stop
- If the EDA in Step 1 shows that, *excluding nationality*, no combination of the remaining features reaches even a modest lift over the base rate (AUC < 0.55), the honest answer is: **do not deploy a model; use the fixed rule from option 1** (short lead-time + free-cancellation offered) and accept the residual cancellation cost. Forcing a model where the signal is weak will just produce a false sense of precision and, worse, a rule that looks data-driven but is actually noise.
- If legal counsel (Step 0) says even the `market` proxy is too close to nationality for the EU market, the model loses that feature and you re-run Step 3. If the remaining features are too weak, fall back to option 1.

# Predicting Refund Risk at Order Placement

## The problem, stated plainly

**The decision:** For each incoming order, customer care decides whether to place a confirmation call before shipping. They will call the orders with the highest predicted refund probability.

**The user of the result:** Your customer-care agents, in real time, one order at a time. They need a single score (or a yes/no flag) and, ideally, a short reason ("high-value electronics order from a first-time customer in Region X") so the call feels natural rather than random.

**The unit and the moment:** One order, scored at the instant it is placed. Only information that exists *before* the package is dispatched may feed the model — no delivery confirmation, no product inspection, no post-shipment interaction.

**What is known (you told me):**
- One row per order; 2,020 rows in the export.
- Columns: order_id, order_date, region, channel, product_category, amount, status, customer_id.
- `status` is the final outcome: the export was pulled six weeks after the last order, and the refund window is 14 days, so no row is still pending.
- The target is binary: refund vs. no refund, read off `status`.

**What is not in the table (I must flag this):**
- No product-level detail beyond the category string.
- No delivery address granularity beyond `region`.
- No payment method, shipping speed, or discount fields.
- No explicit customer-history columns (number of prior orders, prior refund count, account age). I *can* derive some of these from `customer_id` + `order_date` within this same table, but only for customers who already appear in the 2,020 rows. For a brand-new customer at prediction time, those derived features would be zero/missing and must be handled.

**What I assume (you did not state, so I am being explicit):**
- `status` contains at least one value (or a small set of values) that unambiguously means "refunded," distinct from values meaning delivered / completed / cancelled-for-other-reasons. I will confirm the exact labels with you before coding.
- In production you have a customer database where, at order placement, you can look up that customer's past orders and past refunds. The table I see is a snapshot; the live system has the full history.
- Customer care has a finite number of calls it can make per day or per shift. You have not given me that number, so I will express the operating threshold in terms of "top-k orders" and you can set k to capacity.
- The UAE context means I will treat `region` as a domestic sub-region (emirate or zone) rather than a country, and I will check `order_date` for Ramadan / National Day / year-end-sale seasonality.

## Approaches I considered

| # | Approach | What it gives | What it costs / where it struggles |
|---|----------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| A | **No model – slice-and-threshold rules.** Compute the refund rate for every combination of (product_category × region × channel × amount-band). Flag any order falling in a cell whose rate exceeds a chosen percentile. | Zero training pipeline; fully transparent to customer care; ships in a day. | Ignores interactions that span more than two or three slices; fragile when a new category or region appears; cannot incorporate customer history. |
| B | **Logistic regression** (one-hot or target-encoded categoricals, log(amount), customer history counts). | Coefficients are directly explainable ("each additional prior refund raises log-odds by …"); robust at small n; trivial to deploy as a SQL formula or a 20-line script. | Misses non-linear interactions unless you hand-add them; performance plateaus once the true relationship is curved or has high-order interactions. |
| C | **Gradient-boosted decision trees** (LightGBM or sklearn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier). | Handles the mixed types (categoricals + numeric + small derived counts) with little feature engineering; captures interactions automatically; typically the strongest tabular model at 2k rows. | Slightly less transparent (you can still extract feature-importance and SHAP values); a small number of trees and a modest learning rate are needed to avoid overfitting 2,020 rows. |
| D | **Deep / ensemble-of-ensembles, Bayesian nets, etc.** | Marginal accuracy gain if any. | Overkill at 2,020 rows; long tuning time; hard to explain to the care team; high maintenance. Not worth it here. |

**My recommendation:** Build **C (gradient-boosted trees)** as the production model, and keep **B (logistic regression)** as an interpretability companion you can show the care team. Ship **A (rule-based slices)** as a same-week stopgap so the team has *something* while C is validated. Do not pursue D.

## The plan, step by step

### Step 1 – Define the target and confirm labels (half a day)
- Sit with the data owner, list every distinct value in `status`, and agree which map to "refund = 1" and which to "no refund = 0."
- Verify the count of refunds vs. non-refunds so we know the class balance (I will not assume a rate; you have the number).
- Confirm that `status` for every row is truly final (you already told me it is; a 30-second sanity check on the latest-dated rows is cheap insurance).

### Step 2 – Engineer features available at placement (a day)
Work only with fields that exist *before* shipping:

| Source column | Derived feature(s) |
|---|---|
| order_date | day-of-week, is-weekend, month, week-of-year, flags for known UAE sale periods (Eid, National Day, Black-Friday-equivalent) |
| region | keep as categorical |
| channel | keep as categorical |
| product_category | keep as categorical |
| amount | raw value; log₁₀(amount + 1) to reduce skew |
| customer_id | **Prior-order count** for this customer (all orders with date < current order_date); **prior-refund count**; **time since customer's first order**; flag for "first-ever order." For a customer not yet in the system, set counts to 0 and first-order flag to 1. |
| (cross) | Interactions the tree will find on its own (e.g., amount × category) — do not hand-build them for C; do hand-build a couple for B if the regression looks weak. |

Drop `order_id` (pure identifier, no signal).

### Step 3 – Time-based split (part of Step 2)
- Sort all 2,020 rows by `order_date`.
- Train on the earliest ~75 % of dates; hold out the latest ~25 % as a single **test set**. Do **not** shuffle.
- Within the training set, carve a validation slice (last 10–15 % of training dates) for early-stopping and hyper-parameter checks.
- Rationale: this mimics "today's model predicts tomorrow's order" and prevents leakage from future dates.

### Step 4 – Train the primary model (a day)
- **LightGBM** (or `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` if you prefer staying in scikit-learn).
- Conservative hyper-parameters for 2,020 rows: ~100–300 trees, learning rate 0.05, max depth 4–6, minimum samples per leaf ≥ 20. Tune on the validation slice only.
- Let LightGBM ingest `region`, `channel`, `product_category` as native categoricals (no one-hot). Feed numeric features (amount, log-amount, prior counts, date features) as-is.
- Fit the **logistic-regression** companion on the same training split with one-hot categoricals for the explainability readout.
- Record: training accuracy, validation PR-AUC, and the top-10 feature-importance list.

### Step 5 – Evaluate the way the care team will use it (a day)
The question the team asks is not "what is overall accuracy?" but **"if I call the top 5 % (or top 10 %) of orders by score, how many actual refunds do I catch, and how many of my calls are wasted?"**

- On the held-out test set, sort orders by predicted probability (descending).
- Plot the **precision-recall curve** and read off: at top-5 %, top-10 %, top-20 % by score → precision (fraction of called orders that actually refund) and recall (fraction of all test-set refunds that were in the called group).
- Overlay the **rule-based baseline (A)** at its best slice so you can see the lift.
- Check **calibration**: bin predicted probabilities into deciles; compare the average predicted probability in each bin to the observed refund rate. If a "0.30" bin really yields ~30 % refunds, the score is trustworthy and you can set a clean threshold.
- Examine the **logistic-regression coefficients** (or SHAP values from the tree) to sanity-check direction: e.g., does "prior-refund count > 0" push risk up? Does a very high `amount` in a given category push it up? If a sign is backwards, investigate before trusting the model.
- **Stop / go gate:** If the top-10 % precision is not meaningfully above the overall refund rate (or below a threshold *you* set with the care team, e.g., "I need at least 1 in 4 calls to land a refund"), the model is not ready. Go back to Step 2 and look for missing features (payment method, shipping speed, discount) or reconsider the target definition.

### Step 6 – Set the operating policy (with the care team)
- Agree on the daily call budget: "We can make N calls per shift."
- Translate N into a score cutoff on the validation/test distributions (e.g., "call every order scoring above the 90th percentile of the test-set scores").
- Document the policy: score ≥ cutoff → phone the buyer, confirm product spec and delivery address, log the outcome.
- Provide the care team a one-page "why was this order flagged" sheet using the top-3 SHAP contributions per order.

### Step 7 – Deploy and score in production (a day or two of engineering)
- At order-creation time, the order-management system already has: date, region, channel, category, amount, customer_id.
- A lightweight service (a REST endpoint, a stored procedure, or even a pre-computed lookup for the rule-based stopgap) takes those inputs, pulls the customer's prior-order / prior-refund counts from the customer DB, runs the model, and returns a probability in < 100 ms.
- If probability ≥ cutoff → create a task in the care queue with the SHAP reason.

### Step 8 – Monitor, retrain, and know when to stop (ongoing)
- **Weekly:** compare the predicted-vs-actual refund rate in each score decile for the week's scored orders. If calibration drifts more than a few points, flag it.
- **Monthly (or quarterly):** retrain on the rolling window of the most recent orders (keep the time-based split discipline). Track whether the test PR-AUC is holding.
- **Retrigger / stop conditions:**
  - A new `region` or `product_category` appears that was not in training → the model has no learned behaviour for it; either add it and retrain, or fall back to the rule-based slice for that new value.
  - Precision at the operating threshold drops below the agreed floor for two consecutive weeks → pause automated flagging, investigate (seasonal shift? policy change in refund terms?), retrain.
  - Refund rate in the business shifts structurally (e.g., a new 30-day return policy is announced) → the target distribution changes; retrain and re-calibrate.
- **Hard stop:** if after two retrain cycles the model still cannot beat the rule-based baseline at the team's operating point, retire the model and run the rules. Document the decision.

1. The distinct values in `status` and which mean "refunded." (I cannot see them.)
2. The overall refund count or rate, so I can size the class imbalance and set a sensible baseline.
3. The care team's approximate daily call capacity, so I can set the top-k in Step 6.
4. Confirmation that the customer database in production stores full order and refund history per customer_id (so the prior-count features are computable for every customer, not just those in this 2,020-row export).
5. Any known UAE seasonal events you want hard-coded as date flags (Ramadan dates for the relevant year, National Day, etc.).

With those five answers in hand, Steps 1 through 5 are roughly three to four working days of analyst time, and Step 7 is a short hand-off to your engineering team. The rule-based stopgap (A) can be in the care team's hands within a day so they are not flying blind while the model is being built.
